terms.grammar: preposition: with the ablative for where a thing is, with the accusative for where it goes
evidence: Cic. ND 2.95: quī sub terrā semper habitāvissent
Cic. Rep. 1.25: cum tōta sē lūna sub orbem sōlis subjēcisset
terms.comment: The ablative for rest, sub tēctō, under a roof; the accusative for motion, sub orbem sōlis, passing beneath the sun’s disc. Of a hill or a wall, at its foot: sub monte cōnsēdit (Caes. BG 1.48, Lewis & Short). For “below”, lower than, see below (īnfrā, subter).

phrases.latin: quantō est facilius mihi sub tēctō vīvere
phrases.english: how much easier it is for me to live under a roof

phrases.latin: saepe exiguus mūs sub terrīs posuitque domōs atque horrea fēcit
phrases.english: often the tiny mouse has made his home and built his barns beneath the ground
the hunter stays out under the cold sky

phrases.latin: certō illud tempore fierī et necessāriō, cum tōta sē lūna sub orbem sōlis subjēcisset
phrases.english: that this happens at a fixed time and of necessity, when the whole moon has passed beneath the sun’s disc

sources: Lewis & Short: sub
Dickinson: Latin Core Vocabulary

Cicero (De natura deorum 2, De re publica 1), Phaedrus 3, Virgil, Georgics 1 and Horace, Odes 1 checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026); the Phaedrus and Georgics lines are also in the Latinitas loci collections (loci-phaedrus, loci-vergilius-georgica).
Citations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them and have not been checked against an edition.
